I think you may be mixing two different topics here. First is immunity from personal liability and second is preclusion of claims against the government. So, generally speaking no governmental official is personally liable for actions taken within their office. This is why you can sue a city and get money back when a cop beats your ass, but you are unlikely to be able to push the cop into personal bankruptcy. So, yes, the President is immune for acts he takes doing his job.

Relatedly, but somewhat separate is the issue of whether you can sue the government or governmental officials at all. That is a matter of sovereign immunity which traces its way back centuries (and from which the personal immunity discussed above is derived). In practical application, there are many exceptions to the immunity. However, the way most of them are set up, it makes the AG the proper defendant (which is why so many cases against the USG are styled the way they are). While it is possible they messed up this case this case and it could therefore be summarily dismissed, I really doubt that is the case.
